newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia coffee stable, London seen gaining.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia coffee stable, London seen gaining.

text.p: Indonesian coffee prices were stable on Friday, but London futures were seen staging a rebound on the back of gains in New York overnight, traders said.
They also said there had been no news of robusta contract defaults by local firms, who were mostly holding off transactions in anticipation of increases in London later on Friday.
"London is due to rise by $50-$80 at the opening following increases in New York yesterday," one trader said. "Robusta prices are still considered low when compared with arabicas."
New York coffee arabica futures ended broadly higher in choppy trade on Thursday, bolstered by a late-session round of commission house and light trade buying.
Spot July finished 5.85 cents higher at 195.90 cents a lb, while the benchmark September contract rose 4.30 cents to 179.85 cents after ranging from 181.00 to 168.75 cents.
Earlier in the day, London's September robusta contract ended $5 down at $1,860 a tonne while July rebounded from its lows but still ended $27 lower at $1,823.

Indonesian traders said local grade four robusta was quoted at 3,750 rupiah/kg in the key growing region of Lampung in South Sumatra, unchanged from Thursday. The export price was also unchanged at $1,600 a tonne FOB Lampung.
"I have not heard of any local shippers defaulting on their contracts," one trader said. "Everyone has been sticking to their deals despite changes to the prices."
"There have been defaults on arabica contracts but not on robustas...not so far," he said. "I heard one company defaulted on about 300 tonnes of arabica because of the price surge."
Indonesia is the world's third largest coffee producer and the top robusta producer.
Another trader said exporters were scrambling for robusta beans following a shortfall in production due to bad weather earlier this year.
"Production has been affected in the highlands of the Lampung region," he said. "The situation is not that bad in North Sumatra and growing areas on Java island and elsewhere."
The so-called coffee triangle of Lampung, Bengkulu and South Sumatra accounts for some 70 percent of national production.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture in a report issued last Friday projected Indonesian coffee production at 7,600 60-kg bas (456,000 tonnes) in 1996/97 (July-June) and 6,800 bags (408,000 tonnes) in 1997/98.
In contrast, Oesman Soedargo, chairman of the Association of Indonesian Coffee Exporters sees 1997 production plunging by 160,000 tonnes to 290,000 tonnes from 1996.
He said the exportable amount was expected to be around 180,000 tonnes in 1997 against 330,000 tonnes in 1996.
